findings.title: Unguarded Optional.get() produces a 500 when the recovery-code credential cannot be read back
findings.body: `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user)` returns an `Optional`, but the bean immediately calls `credentialModelOpt.get()` (and then `getNextRecoveryAuthnCode().get()`). With the new user-storage support, a provider can legitimately report `isConfiguredFor(recovery-authn-codes) == true` (so `RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator.configuredFor()` shows the form) while exposing no credential object at all through `getFederatedCredentialsStream()`/`getCredentials()` – that is exactly the default for any existing `CredentialInputUpdater` that does not implement credential listing. In that case the Optional is empty and rendering the login page throws `NoSuchElementException`, which surfaces as an internal server error instead of a login form. The bean should handle the empty case (e.g. fall back to code number 0 / a generic prompt) rather than dereferencing blindly.

findings.title: New user-storage credential contract for recovery codes is undocumented and asymmetric
findings.body: `createRecoveryCodesCredential()` hands the user-storage provider a `UserCredentialModel` of type `recovery-authn-codes` whose value is a JSON array of all 12 *raw* codes, while validation (`UserCredentialModel.buildFromBackupAuthnCode()` in `RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator`) hands the same provider a single raw code with dashes stripped. Nothing in the javadoc or in any SPI documentation states this format, that the codes arrive unhashed (so the provider is responsible for hashing them), or that the provider must mark a code consumed after a successful validation. Third-party providers implementing `CredentialInputUpdater.supportsCredentialType(recovery-authn-codes)` will silently store/compare the wrong thing. Please document the expected serialization and the one-time-use obligation on this method (and ideally use a stable constant instead of the hardcoded provider id "keycloak-recovery-authn-codes").

findings.title: User label and generation timestamp are dropped when codes go to user storage
findings.body: The `UserCredentialModel` built here carries only the type and the JSON of the raw codes. The `credentialModel` argument, which holds the user-supplied label (`userLabel`) and the `generatedAt` timestamp collected by `RecoveryAuthnCodesAction`, is only used for its type on the user-storage path and is discarded. As a result a user who names their recovery-code set loses that label whenever the credential ends up in the user storage (the test provider indeed returns `getUserLabel() == null`), and the created date becomes the provider's own clock value rather than the generation time shown to the user.

findings.title: removeStoredCredentialById() is now called with an id that may come from (or be missing in) user storage
findings.body: After the switch to `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential()`, `optUserCredentialFound` may be a credential returned by the user-storage provider via `getFederatedCredentialsStream()`. Its id is not a local/federated-store credential id, and in the reference implementation added in this PR (`BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.getCredentials`, which builds the model with `createFromValues` and never copies the id) it is `null`. Calling `authenticatedUser.credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById(null/foreign-id)` therefore cannot delete the exhausted credential: it silently no-ops (or fails), while the user is pushed into the CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES required action. The exhausted credential stays in the user storage and the new one is written on top of it, so state can diverge. The removal path needs to distinguish federated credentials from locally stored ones.

findings.title: getCredentials() NPEs for users not present in the provider map
findings.body: `getCredentials()` does `var myUser = getMyUser(user); if (myUser.recoveryCodes != null)` with no null check, unlike every sibling method (`getDisableableCredentialTypesStream`, `isConfiguredFor`, `isValid`) which all guard against `getMyUser(user) == null`. Because this method is reached from `credentialManager().getFederatedCredentialsStream()` (account console credential listing, the new `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential()`), any call for a user id that is no longer in the in-memory map (removed user, stale cache entry, different factory instance) throws a NullPointerException out of the provider instead of returning an empty stream.

findings.title: Recovery-code credential exposed by getCredentials() has no id
findings.body: `updateCredential()` assigns `recoveryCodesModel.setId(KeycloakModelUtils.generateId())`, but `getCredentials()` rebuilds the model with `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues(...)`, which does not set an id, and the stored id is never copied over. Consumers of `getFederatedCredentialsStream()` therefore see a credential with `id == null`: the account console renders/deletes credentials by id, and `RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator` calls `removeStoredCredentialById(model.getId())` with that null. The same bug was explicitly fixed for OTP in this diff (`newOTP.setId(...)`), so the recovery-code model should propagate the id too.

findings.title: Reference provider never invalidates a used recovery code, so one-time-use is not covered by any test
findings.body: `isValid()` for `recovery-authn-codes` simply checks whether the submitted value is contained in the stored plaintext list and returns true, without removing/marking the code as used. Consequently the same recovery code can be replayed an unlimited number of times against this provider, and the new integration test (`testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin`) cannot detect that the critical one-time-use semantics of recovery codes are preserved when the credential lives in user storage. Please consume the code on successful validation (and add an assertion that re-using the same code fails, and that the next login asks for the following code number).

findings.title: supportsCredentialType()/isConfiguredFor() can NPE on a null credential type
findings.body: The new conditions are written as `credentialType.equals(RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE)` (lines 114 and 275), dereferencing the parameter. The pre-existing checks in the same expressions (`CredentialModel.PASSWORD.equals(credentialType)`, `isOTPType(...)`) are null-safe, so a null type used to be handled gracefully and now throws NullPointerException. Invert the comparison to `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE.equals(credentialType)`.

findings.title: Recovery codes stored in the provider cannot be disabled/removed
findings.body: `disableCredentialType()` only clears OTP and `getDisableableCredentialTypesStream()` only reports `CredentialModel.OTP`, yet `getCredentials()` now exposes the recovery-code credential to the account console and admin REST. The credential is therefore listed but there is no way to delete or disable it through the standard credential-management paths, which also means the new feature has no test for removing user-storage recovery codes (the OTP equivalent is covered by `testOTPSetupAndRemoveThroughAccountMgmtAndLogin`).

findings.title: Login is never completed and logout result is ignored in testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin
findings.body: Unlike the sibling tests, this test never calls `testAppHelper.completeLogin()` after submitting the recovery code, so the authorization code is never exchanged and no tokens (incl. the id/refresh token used by `TestAppHelper.logout()`) are obtained. The subsequent `testAppHelper.logout()` is then very likely a no-op/failure and its boolean result is discarded (other tests use `assertTrue(testAppHelper.logout())`). The result is that the test neither verifies a complete, token-producing login via a user-storage recovery code nor reliably tears the SSO session down, which can leak session state into the other tests in this class that log in as the same user `otp1`.
